{"phase":"draft","role":"workflow","sealed_request":{"assistance":{"background":"","depth":"overview","direction":"overview","follow_up":"Explain ReAct's mechanism and what its excerpts cannot establish.","mode":"learn"},"kind":"deep_dive","private_context":{"notes":false,"profile":false,"reading_history":false},"project_context":null,"schema_revision":"workspace-assistance-purpose-specific-v2","settings":{"effort":"medium","max_repairs":1,"structured_outputs":true,"temperature":null,"thinking":{"type":"between_tools"}},"units":{"ua6f0f4d05fd72b2b86b2":{"end":3379,"material_id":"mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2","page":6,"parser_revision":"workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1","quote":"B) While interleaving reasoning, action and observation steps improves ReAct’s grounded-
ness and trustworthiness, such a structural constraint also reduces its ﬂexibility in formulating
reasoning steps, leading to more reasoning error rate than CoT. we note that there is one frequent
error pattern speciﬁc to ReAct, in which the model repetitively generates the previous thoughts and
actions, and we categorize it as part of “reasoning error” as the model fails to reason about what the
proper next action to take and jump out of the loop4.

  C) For ReAct, successfully retrieving informative knowledge via search is critical. Non-
informative search, which counts for 23% of the error cases, derails the model reasoning and gives
it a hard time to recover and reformulate thoughts. This is perhaps an expected trade-off between
factuality and ﬂexibility, which motivates our proposed strategies of combining two methods.

We provide examples for each success and failure modes in Appendix E.1. We also ﬁnd some
HotpotQA questions may contain outdated answer labels, see Figure 4 for example.

ReAct + CoT-SC perform best for prompting LLMs  Also shown in Table 1, the best prompting
method on HotpotQA and Fever are ReAct →CoT-SC and CoT-SC →ReAct respectively.
Furthermore, Figure 2 shows how different methods perform with respect to the number of CoT-SC
samples used.","scope":"excerpt","source_hash":"sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69","span_id":"span-b615625987cdbfe74682109ab6dc0e19","start":2005,"version_id":"arxiv:2210.03629:v3","work_id":"arxiv:2210.03629"}}}}

{"phase":"draft","role":"workflow","sealed_request":{"assistance":{"background":"","depth":"overview","direction":"overview","follow_up":"Compare ReAct and Self-RAG evidence and evaluation limitations.","mode":"research"},"kind":"deep_dive","private_context":{"notes":false,"profile":false,"reading_history":false},"project_context":{"constraints":"No private notes, no source expansion; retained scopes only","id":"project-d323fc7f292539ea490d65421aa0ea75","question":"Compare ReAct and Self-RAG evidence and evaluation limitations.","revision":1,"scope":"Declared public retained corpus only"},"schema_revision":"workspace-assistance-purpose-specific-v2","settings":{"effort":"medium","max_repairs":1,"structured_outputs":true,"temperature":null,"thinking":{"type":"between_tools"}},"units":{"u423a5ed5c10153d66367":{"end":3616,"material_id":"mat-f98fbd73f423776117f60cac36edc90a","page":3,"parser_revision":"workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1","quote":"While their value function
simply indicates an overall score of each generation, SELF-RAG trains to an arbitrary LM to learn to
generate fine-grained self-reflection and customizable inference.

Training and generating with critics. Training LLMs with reinforcement learning (e.g., Proximal
Policy Optimization or PPO; Schulman et al. 2017) from human feedback (RLHF) has proven
effective in aligning LLMs with human preferences (Ouyang et al., 2022). Wu et al. (2023) introduce
fine-grained RLHF with multiple reward models. Though our work also studies fine-grained critique
on retrieval and generation, we train our target LM on task examples augmented with reflection
tokens from a critic model offline, with a far lower training cost compared to RLHF. In addition,
reflection tokens in SELF-RAG enable controllable generation at inference, while RLHF focuses on
human preference alignment during training. Other works use general control tokens to guide LM
generation (Lu et al., 2022; Korbak et al., 2023), while SELF-RAG uses reflection tokens to decide the
need for retrieval and to self-evaluate generation quality. Xie et al. (2023) propose a self-evaluation-
guided decoding framework, but they focus only on reasoning tasks with one evaluation dimension
(reasoning path consistency) and without retrieval. Recent work on LLM refinement (Dhuliawala
et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Paul et al., 2023) prompts a model to generate task output, natural
language feedback and refined task output iteratively, but at the cost of inference efficiency.","scope":"excerpt","source_hash":"sha256:d9eaa1398abac0df67a9d0933a5bf8b6d9d83d2e72da2a486073cd842dd52978","span_id":"span-f021c711415ab7488317517d7cbe41d5","start":2058,"version_id":"arxiv:2310.11511:v1","work_id":"arxiv:2310.11511"},"uf800ed16cb52eb251690":{"end":3888,"material_id":"mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2","page":1,"parser_revision":"workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1","quote":"Furthermore, on two interactive decision making benchmarks (ALFWorld and
                           WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by
                            an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with
                              only one or two in-context examples.


                1  INTRODUCTION

              A unique feature of human intelligence is the ability to seamlessly combine task-oriented actions with
                        verbal reasoning (or inner speech, Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2015), which has been theorized toarXiv:2210.03629v3                      play an important role in human cognition for enabling self-regulation or strategization (Vygotsky,
                     1987; Luria, 1965; Fernyhough, 2010) and maintaining a working memory (Baddeley, 1992). Con-
                         sider the example of cooking up a dish in the kitchen. Between any two speciﬁc actions, we may
                       reason in language in order to track progress (“now that everything is cut, I should heat up the pot of
                        water”), to handle exceptions or adjust the plan according to the situation (“I don’t have salt, so let
                me use soy sauce and pepper instead”), and to realize when external information is needed (“how do
                             I prepare dough? Let me search on the Internet”).","scope":"excerpt","source_hash":"sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69","span_id":"span-55b2971cd5f40c431b738813c7ef10cd","start":2443,"version_id":"arxiv:2210.03629:v3","work_id":"arxiv:2210.03629"}}}}

messages.content: {"phase":"draft","role":"workflow","sealed_request":{"assistance":{"background":"","depth":"overview","direction":"overview","follow_up":"How do retrieval and incomplete relevance judgments affect RAG evaluation?","mode":"research"},"kind":"deep_dive","private_context":{"notes":false,"profile":false,"reading_history":false},"project_context":{"constraints":"No private notes, no source expansion; retained scopes only","id":"project-37e7c1c6eb4ddc27b857078580b52dd7","question":"How do retrieval and incomplete relevance judgments affect RAG evaluation?","revision":1,"scope":"Declared public retained corpus only"},"schema_revision":"workspace-assistance-purpose-specific-v2","settings":{"effort":"medium","max_repairs":1,"structured_outputs":true,"temperature":null,"thinking":{"type":"between_tools"}},"units":{"u1aab0740f44dab2c5010":{"end":1545,"material_id":"mat-a722330404855072b6b7fb9b13004998","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"Conversational RAG benchmarks such as MTRAG and RETECO evaluate retrieval and generation end to end: each system answers from its own retrieval, so abstention must be scored against whether each retrieved context is sufficient. A convenient shortcut reads sufficiency off the relevance judgments and treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable. We re-run the official baselines exactly and test this shortcut on RECOR (RETECO track~2) with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model of another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication. The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28\\% to 72\\%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). A reader agrees: Qwen3-4B answers 62--67\\% of these false misses correctly, against 23--30\\% of no-gold contexts judged insufficient and 1\\% with no documents. In most false misses, the answer comes from a hard negative mined for the same question, another turn's gold or a neighbouring chunk of the gold page. On MTRAG, whose judgments come from annotators, precision drops from .72 to .50. Under the shortcut, answerability AUROC is up to .19 too low, and the best sufficiency detector appears to be a retrieval score that never reads the documents. We release code, runs and labels, and recommend scoring refusals against content labels, not the presence of gold.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:001a0cb486d1e1a1081cc92155eb757b894e9d7b1633615d5b311dff7ce64cc3","span_id":"span-6e05d19768ccb5f09cbbbbd979e4bd9e","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.40966:v1:metadata-55c0a56c8750035c","work_id":"arxiv:2610.40966"},"ubd07e5a5c1c7b28702f5":{"end":1567,"material_id":"mat-3d7daff77ffce12e7f3ebd3ca37934de","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"Digital agents can now gather and organize information, reason over it, and use tools to complete complex tasks. Forecasting puts all of these abilities to the test: it requires integrating incomplete evidence, inferring causal drivers, and committing to calibrated probabilistic judgments. Existing benchmarks are poorly suited to measuring and improving this ability. Live benchmarks provide feedback only after events resolve, so every evaluation cycle waits on the calendar; fixed-corpus evaluations return results immediately but confine research to pre-collected documents. We introduce FABench, a scalable backtesting environment for Forecasting Agents. An automated pipeline discovers events, generates questions, and resolves outcomes for any past forecast date, so the benchmark can be renewed to stay ahead of model training cutoffs; its first release poses 287 questions across nine domains. Agents research each question freely in an archive environment that combines an offline archive with live web search screened to prevent temporal leakage. Evaluating agents built on eight recent models, we find that retrieval improves the Brier score of all eight in every retrieval setting and lifts the leading agents to the market consensus on the 54 questions linked to Polymarket, with the best three scoring slightly above it. Research traces reveal recurring failures in how agents weigh and apply evidence, leaving ample room for improvement. We release our code, data, and archive environment as a foundation for community research on forecasting agents.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:7508dbee3d2508303bc3d7a5bf7053d68f211ba7def405cf8046d5bcb44efb87","span_id":"span-0bb2e4eacf688b11bbeee4fd8fc02305","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.40940:v1:metadata-21d8200059afcd01","work_id":"arxiv:2610.40940"}}}}

messages.content: {"phase":"draft","role":"workflow","sealed_request":{"assistance":{"background":"","depth":"overview","direction":"overview","follow_up":"Does reinforcement learning control evidence establish safe deployment on my unspecified hardware?","mode":"research"},"kind":"deep_dive","private_context":{"notes":false,"profile":false,"reading_history":false},"project_context":{"constraints":"No private notes, no source expansion; retained scopes only","id":"project-1dc80bbcab7482f86636144447a50782","question":"Does reinforcement learning control evidence establish safe deployment on my unspecified hardware?","revision":1,"scope":"Declared public retained corpus only"},"schema_revision":"workspace-assistance-purpose-specific-v2","settings":{"effort":"medium","max_repairs":1,"structured_outputs":true,"temperature":null,"thinking":{"type":"between_tools"}},"units":{"u279d7c2fd96be4c34489":{"end":1400,"material_id":"mat-57a15743d7b145d492ea35b8ba375944","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:7278e7855992f1f491d61753f082dc9884a7be3cbda3dadad8a22efa258b0646","span_id":"span-d851104d65a3eee8be5928bc37e9dd7b","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.41022:v1:metadata-1d7490e908ceb729","work_id":"arxiv:2610.41022"},"ucbe894d1356a18e9f328":{"end":875,"material_id":"mat-54f2f6e0645f499458d5030d06e35a59","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:2b307ec864315d90d5e828786c2505fff1feda8837559b7e8601961ea9717759","span_id":"span-3fd278aadaa92873179ed21c075ab368","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.41482:v1:metadata-e5c832a06d88973f","work_id":"arxiv:2610.41482"}}}}
